brief_item.title: Kairos：负载感知Prefill重定向调度器面向解耦推理
brief_item.core_conclusion: 解耦推理Prefill排队而Decode空闲，Kairos预测TTFT并把部分Prefill重定向到Decode节点就地执行，以此消除跨节点KV传输。
brief_item.mechanism: 调度器逐请求算预期TTFT与各Decode节点的TBT安全分块进度，仅当更快且满足SLO时转向。
brief_item.result: Bursty负载上P95 TTFT最多降81%，9 RPS内同时满足双SLO而两基线均违约。
brief_item.boundary: 仅小集群单一MoE模型与单一trace，峰值收益为曲线读数。
brief_item.project_relevance: 状态感知调度能利用Decode余量消除KV传输，可作解耦推理SLO调度参照。

facts.title: Towards Load-Aware Prefill Deflection for Disaggregated LLM Serving
facts.event_hint: Kairos: a proactive prefill-deflecting scheduler for disaggregated LLM serving (on vLLM 0.18.1) that reroutes a request's prefill phase to a decode node as chunked-prefill steps interleaved with in-flight decodes, eliminating the inter-node KV transfer for deflected requests; evaluated on the Bursty production-derived trace with DeepSeek-V2-Lite against PD Disaggregation and TaiChi on Azure A100 nodes.
facts.problem: Disaggregated LLM serving (Splitwise, DistServe, Mooncake, TetriInfer) runs prefill and decode on separate GPU pools, but under bursty, heavy-tailed workloads prefill nodes saturate and queue while decode nodes run underutilized (decode is memory-bound and leaves compute slack unused). On a production-style 2P2D A100 cluster, prefill execution accounts for only 2-23% of P95 TTFT; the remaining 77-98% is prefill queue wait and inter-node GPU-GPU KV-cache transfer. Static threshold-based deflection policies leave performance on the table.
facts.mechanism: Kairos is a proactive prefill-deflecting scheduler (approx. 2000 lines of Python on vLLM 0.18.1, per-request overhead <1 ms via Algorithm 1's deflection-decision loop) that lets a decode node execute a queued request's prefill phase as chunked-prefill steps interleaved with its in-flight decode batch; because the deflected request's prefill runs in place on the decode node, the inter-node KV transfer is eliminated. For each queued request the Dispatcher computes: (1) expected prefill-node TTFT = queue wait + prefill time (Eq. 1); (2) for each decode node, a TBT-safe chunk schedule built by greedily picking the largest safe chunk via LargestSafe (Eq. 5) and summing step latencies (Eq. 6); (3) deflects to the fastest feasible decode node iff its projected TTFT <= alpha * prefill-node TTFT AND <= TTFT_SLO (Eq. 7). TBT safety is enforced by three closed-form analytical step-latency predictors (prefill, decode, mixed batches) plus a transfer-time model, all fit by one-time profiling per model-hardware combination and validated at MAPE < 10% on held-out traces. Single operator knob alpha>=1 (alpha=1 deflects only when strictly faster; alpha>1 allows bounded TTFT regression to relieve the prefill queue within the request's own TTFT SLO). Decode nodes report updated (B_n, K_n) state every heartbeat (Delta_h = 100ms).

evidence.claim: P95 TTFT breakdown on the 2P2D A100 cluster (DeepSeek-V2-Lite, normalized production trace): prefill execution is only 2-23% of end-to-end P95 TTFT across all five workloads; the rest is prefill queue wait + inter-node KV-cache transfer. E.g. Bursty P95 TTFT 7893.9 ms = prefill queue 840.8 + prefill exec 1070.1 + KV transfer 2175.6 + decode queue 55.6 ms; LPLD P95 6278.8 ms with KV transfer alone 4205.4 ms; HPHD KV transfer 3584.6 ms.
evidence.value: prefill exec 2-23% of P95 TTFT; KV transfer up to 4.2s P95 (LPLD), 3.5s (HPHD), 2.1s (Bursty)
evidence.baseline: measured prefill execution share within end-to-end P95 TTFT
evidence.condition: 2P2D A100 80GB, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, five production-derived workloads (LPLD/LPHD/HPLD/HPHD/Bursty)
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 5 (Table 3 P95 TTFT breakdown); PDF Page 4 (Claim 2)

evidence.claim: Complementary utilization (Table 2): across all workloads prefill SM utilization is 75-84% while decode SM utilization never exceeds 27% (LPHD peak 26.4%; HPLD as low as 7.5%); prefill HBM BW use under 1.6% of A100 2TB/s peak and decode under 1%, confirming prefill is compute-bound and decode leaves compute slack.
evidence.value: prefill SM 75-84%; decode SM <=27%; prefill BW <1.6% peak; decode BW <1% peak
evidence.condition: steady-state on 2P2D cluster, mean +/- s.d. over five workloads

evidence.claim: Evaluation setup and baselines (Section 6.1): experiments on Azure ML Standard_ND96amsr_A100_v4 nodes (8x A100-SXM4-80GB per node, NVLink 3.0, AMD EPYC 7V12 64-core, 900 GiB host memory, InfiniBand + Azure Accelerated Networking for inter-node); model DeepSeek-V2-Lite (16B total / 2.4B active MoE) on the Bursty trace; SLO targets P95 TTFT <= 4s and P95 TBT <= 70ms (both must hold simultaneously). Two named baselines: PD Disaggregation (DistServe-style, all prefill on prefill nodes) and TaiChi (unified aggregation/disaggregation with differentiated instances and flowing-decode scheduling).
evidence.value: Azure ND96amsr_A100_v4 (8x A100-SXM4-80GB/node, NVLink 3.0, IB); DeepSeek-V2-Lite 16B/2.4B-active; SLO P95 TTFT<=4s & P95 TBT<=70ms; baselines PD Disaggregation + TaiChi
evidence.condition: Bursty production-derived trace, DeepSeek-V2-Lite

evidence.claim: Q1 tail-latency result (Figure 4): on the Bursty trace across RPS 6-12, Kairos stays within both P95 TTFT and P95 TBT SLO up to 9 RPS, while PD Disaggregation and TaiChi violate both TTFT and TBT SLO at high request rates (TaiChi violates both); Kairos's deflection decision loop completes in <1 ms per request.
evidence.value: Kairos within SLO up to 9 RPS; baselines violate TTFT/TBT SLO at high RPS; <1 ms per-request decision
evidence.condition: Bursty trace, RPS 6-12, P95 TTFT<=4s & P95 TBT<=70ms
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 9 (Section 6.2 Q1, Figure 4); PDF Page 9 (Algorithm 1 narrative)

evidence.claim: Predictor accuracy and design (Section 5.2): three closed-form analytical step-latency predictors (prefill, decode, mixed) plus a transfer-time model, each requiring only one-time profiling per model-hardware pair; on held-out traces from Table 1 both step-latency predictors achieve MAPE < 10%, sufficient to reliably rank (chunk size, decode node) pairs. Related-systems comparison (Table 5) positions Kairos's per-request TBT-safe chunk-sweep deflection against Sarathi (intra-node token chunking), Nexus (intra-GPU SM partition), PPD (cross-node append-prefill for Turn 2+), TaiChi, Splitwise, DistServe.
evidence.value: step-latency predictors MAPE < 10%; one-time profiling per model-hardware pair
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V2-Lite on A100
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 6 (Section 5.2 Analytical models); PDF Page 9 (Table 5)

facts.evaluation_context: Production cluster: 2 prefill + 2 decode nodes (2P2D), each NVIDIA A100 80GB (compared against 1P3D and 3P1D on Bursty: 1P3D saturates the single prefill node with median prefill queue >2x 2P2D; 3P1D is decode-capacity-limited with KV-cache-occupancy transfer back-pressure). Evaluation hardware: Azure ML Standard_ND96amsr_A100_v4 nodes, 8x A100-SXM4-80GB per node, NVLink 3.0, AMD EPYC 7V12 64-core, 900 GiB host memory, InfiniBand + Azure Accelerated Networking for inter-node communication. Model: DeepSeek-V2-Lite (16B total / 2.4B active MoE). Evaluated workload: Bursty trace (long-tailed production distribution, Gamma inter-arrivals), the most realistic of the five traces. SLO: P95 TTFT <= 4s AND P95 TBT <= 70ms simultaneously. Baselines: PD Disaggregation (DistServe-style) and TaiChi (unified agg/disagg with flowing-decode scheduling). Dispatcher: per-request Algorithm 1 sweep completes in <1 ms; decode nodes report state every heartbeat Delta_h=100ms. Headline -81% P95 TTFT / +79% SLO attainment are reported as 'up to' maxima over the Bursty trace RPS range.
facts.limitations: The supplement names the baselines (PD Disaggregation = DistServe-style, TaiChi) and hardware and shows Kairos holds SLO up to 9 RPS while baselines violate it, but it does not provide a clean per-RPS table with the exact P95 TTFT (ms) and SLO attainment (%) values behind the headline -81%/+79% maxima; those maxima are read off the Figure 4 curves and the Q2/Q3 results (referenced but the full per-workload improvement table is still beyond the combined visible evidence). Scope: small 2P2D cluster on Azure A100 nodes with DeepSeek-V2-Lite only on the Bursty trace; larger clusters, other models, and non-MoE architectures are not tested. The <1 ms routing overhead is per-request and excludes one-time deployment-time profiling; the centralized dispatcher could become a CPU bottleneck at very high RPS (mitigation: shard by node groups, sacrificing global optimality). Single-deflection-per-heartbeat limit (a decode node accepts one deflected request per 100ms heartbeat); this becomes a bottleneck only at RPS >= |decode nodes| / Delta_h >= 20, above the SLO-supported RPS. Kairos does not account for prefix-cache residency: deflecting a request loses any prefix already cached on the prefill node. KV-transfer elimination applies only to deflected requests; non-deflected requests still incur inter-node KV transfer. RDMA/InfiniBand assumed.
facts.project_relevance: Highly relevant to the TPN card's questions: (1) Kairos is explicitly state-aware — it computes per-request expected TTFT and per-decode-node TBT headroom at scheduling time and deflects based on a TTFT/TBT condition, directly addressing whether the scheduler senses inference phase and KV position; (2) it targets the KV-cache cross-node transfer cost (the dominant 77-98% remainder of P95 TTFT) by eliminating the inter-node KV transfer for deflected requests; (3) it reports end-to-end P95 TTFT and SLO attainment vs named baselines (PD Disaggregation, TaiChi) on the Bursty trace, not just microbenchmarks. It is a concrete answer to what scheduler-side, KV-aware deflection adds over pure GPU-memory scheduling: it exploits decode-side compute slack to remove the transfer that GPU-memory scheduling alone cannot. Caveat: the small 2P2D scale, single Bursty trace, and the 'up to' headline maxima read off Figure 4 still bound the deployable magnitude claim.

facts.title: CodeNib: A Multi-View Data System for Serving Repository Context to Coding Agents
facts.event_hint: CodeNib: a multi-view repository-context data system that materializes reusable lexical (BM25/Zoekt), dense (FAISS), and structural (graph) views per commit, incrementally maintains selected-view deltas across edits, and serves ranked search, symbol navigation, and bounded context through one runtime (with stdio MCP + LSP-shaped skill adapters) to coding agents.
facts.problem: Coding agents repeatedly search, navigate, and retain context from evolving repositories, but today's indexes, language servers, and task-local histories are disconnected: they force repeated discovery, do not map outputs back to a common commit and repository-relative source range, and obscure lifecycle costs (per-edit rebuild vs incremental maintenance). Three coupled challenges: C1 heterogeneous views (lexical/dense/structural need different physical layouts but must map to the same commit and source ranges); C2 incremental freshness (an edit changes each view differently, so graph repair, embedding reuse, and rebuild paths must be selected and evaluated separately); C3 agent delivery (serving bounded context through agent tools).
facts.mechanism: CodeNib builds three reusable views per repository commit: lexical (BM25, optional Zoekt), dense (file-level L0 and callable-level L2 embeddings in FAISS), and structural (a reference graph used for dependency/definition/reference/route navigation). Outputs are mapped to repository-relative path/start-line ranges. Selected views are maintained across edits via incremental delta maintenance (graph repair, embedding reuse, rebuild paths chosen per view). One runtime serves search_semantic/search_bm25/search_regex/search_zoekt, structural tools (dependency subgraphs, definitions, references, routes), and get_manifest; missing optional indexes return explicit tool errors rather than silent fallback. Adapters: stdio MCP (instantiates static serving; exposes semantic/BM25/regex/Zoekt search + structural tools) and LSP-shaped skills (accept an injected static or live JSON-RPC provider, sharing the agent-facing location schema while traces record which backend served). AgentRunner separates index-backed SkillRegistry capabilities from ordinary ToolRegistry primitives; AgentRunTrace records ordered events/context state and UsageTracker records provider tokens. Two context policies are studied: Eager (keeps its prefix throughout) and Compact (deterministically resets the prefix once, after the complete tool batch containing the first successful read, restoring the clean issue + deduped paths + newest successful read + a 600-char direction cue copied from the latest nonempty assistant message; this transition is the policy's single cache discontinuity).

evidence.claim: Agent context-policy token/localization results (Q5, Figure 11a-b), five models (Claude Haiku 4.5, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-27B, Gemma 4-12B, Gemini 2.5 Flash), ordinary tools, 16-turn cap, frozen top-10 candidates, paired grep/read baseline (baseline volume 25.9-159.7K tokens/query). The selected context policy (Eager for Haiku, Compact otherwise) uses 49.9, 45.1, 44.8, 12.9, and 35.8% of paired grep/read tokens respectively (i.e. 50.1-87.1% fewer trajectory tokens). delta-AnswerRecall@5 ranges from -0.009 to +0.067, with all lower bounds above -0.05 (the no-change margin), so localization is preserved versus paired grep/read.
evidence.value: selected policy uses 12.9-49.9% of grep/read tokens (50.1-87.1% fewer); delta-AR@5 -0.009 to +0.067, all >= -0.05
evidence.condition: five models, 16-turn cap, frozen top-10 candidates, Eager/Compact selection rule, full provider-reported trajectories, zero recall for invalid answers

evidence.claim: Compaction is not uniformly dominant (Q5): Compact/Eager token usage ranges from 123.3% (Haiku) to 27.9% (Gemma) of paired grep/read; Gemma and Gemini trade 0.070 and 0.044 AnswerRecall@5 against Eager while still clearing the baseline gate. Workload effects (panel c, descriptive only, several quality intervals cross the margin, so no subgroup-routing claim) span query types (Behavioral 175, File hint 76, Module hint 75, Reasoning 50, Symbol hint 50, Traversal 74) and five languages (C/C++, Go, Python, Rust, TS/JS, 100 each).
evidence.value: Compact/Eager token 27.9-123.3% of grep/read; Gemma/Gemini trade 0.070/0.044 AR@5 vs Eager; no subgroup-routing claim
evidence.condition: five models, descriptive pooled workload/language slices

evidence.claim: Static vs live symbol-navigation latency (Q3, Figure 9): across 1,000 requests over 100 snapshots, 632 (63.2%) normalized path/start-line sets match the live JSON-RPC provider (437/500 definitions = 87.4%; 195/500 references = 39.0%). On the matching subset, static/live p50 = 0.62/2.26 ms, a median paired saving of 1.69 ms and a median live/static ratio of 4.72x. Match rate is the limiting result: definitions 80-99% across languages, references 22-73%.
evidence.value: 63.2% overall match; static p50 0.62 ms vs live 2.26 ms; median live/static 4.72x; def match 87.4%, ref match 39.0%
evidence.baseline: live JSON-RPC language servers (clangd, gopls, basedpyright, rust-analyzer, typescript-language-server)
evidence.condition: 100 snapshots, 1,000 requests (500 def + 500 ref), normalized path/start-line equality on matching subset only

evidence.claim: Incremental update speedup (Section 11 / Appendix F): on transitions matching an independent rebuild, graph-repair and vector-reuse reach 8.67x and 25.44x median speedups respectively (Section 11 conclusion); an independent Rust/TS rebuild cross-check reaches 99.75% median edge F1 and 99.35% serving agreement, and all 31 vector targets match artifact identities and vectors. Appendix G: each materialization uses an isolated quiescent checkout and fresh processes (warm-host, not cold-start; host caches not flushed, remote model weights not reloaded); the evaluated vector builder materializes both L0 and L2 even though the trace queries only L2, so lifecycle cost includes both.
evidence.value: graph-repair 8.67x median; vector-reuse 25.44x median; rebuild F1 99.75%, serving agreement 99.35%; 31/31 vector targets exact
evidence.condition: transitions matching independent rebuild; warm-host materialization, isolated checkout/fresh processes
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 15 (Section 11 Conclusion); PDF Page 22 (Appendix F, Appendix G Lifecycle Execution Boundary)

evidence.claim: Lifecycle session-cost projection (Appendix G Panel c): at q=20 controlled-trace scale, process-isolated and shared-resident projections are 13.20 s/session (95% CI 10.43-15.96) and 6.24 s/session (3.66-8.11); at q=100, medians are 8.53 and 1.27 s/session. Runtime view loading floors the process-isolated model; the shared-resident model approaches measured serve-only S/N, not a hardware floor. Only q=20 is the controlled trace scale; other q values project the same measured terms.
evidence.value: q=20: 13.20/6.24 s/session (process-isolated/shared-resident); q=100: 8.53/1.27 s/session
evidence.baseline: process-isolated vs shared-resident runtime view loading
evidence.condition: lifecycle trace S over N=20 sessions, warm-host, one warmup + three measured repetitions
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 22 (Appendix G Lifecycle Execution Boundary, Panel c)

facts.evaluation_context: 100 repository snapshots (C/C++, Go, Python, Rust, TS/JS). Views: lexical (BM25, optional Zoekt), dense (FAISS IndexFlatIP/IVFFlat/HNSWFlat; L0 file-level and L2 callable-level; five embedders SR-Small 137M, Qwen3-Embed-0.6B, Jina-Code-1.5B, Qwen3-Embed-4B, SR-Large 7B), structural (reference graph). Live comparators: clangd, gopls, basedpyright, rust-analyzer, typescript-language-server. Agent runs: five models (Claude Haiku 4.5, Qwen3.5-9B via vLLM 0.23.0 65K cap, Qwen3.5-27B via vLLM 0.23.0 65K cap, Gemma 4-12B via vLLM 0.25.1 131K cap, Gemini 2.5 Flash via Vertex AI thinkingBudget=0); ordinary tools, 16-turn cap, frozen top-10 candidates, 48K-token history, 4096-token completion, prefix caching; two context policies Eager (keeps prefix) and Compact (resets prefix once). Token axes sum provider-reported prompt/completion tokens (not cache-adjusted); zero recall for invalid answers. Retrieval/index params frozen per Table 7 (graph weight 0.5, RRF constant 60, HNSW M=32 ef_construction=200, IVF probes swept). Lifecycle: isolated quiescent checkout, fresh processes, warm-host (caches not flushed, weights not reloaded); the evaluated vector builder materializes both L0 and L2 even though only L2 is queried.
facts.limitations: The supplement confirms the Q5 agent-loop token reduction: the selected context policy uses 12.9-49.9% of paired grep/read tokens (50.1-87.1% fewer) across the five named models with delta-AnswerRecall@5 all >= -0.05, so the abstract's '50-87% fewer trajectory tokens with localization preserved' is now verified (not just a claim). However: (1) compaction is not uniformly dominant (Compact/Eager token usage ranges 27.9-123.3% of grep/read; Haiku is worse than grep/read at 123.3%) and Gemma/Gemini trade 0.070/0.044 AR@5 against Eager; (2) token axes are provider-reported prompt/completion sums, NOT cache-adjusted cost, and cache hits/prefill latency are unmeasured, so the token reduction may not translate linearly to $/latency; (3) the Compact transition is the policy's single cache discontinuity and the authors do not claim the pre-transition cache survives it; (4) workload-effect slices (panel c) are descriptive with intervals crossing the margin, so no subgroup-routing claim is made; (5) the static-vs-live 4.72x latency ratio applies only to the 63.2% matching subset (references match as little as 22-33%); (6) ANN speedups remain component-local; (7) lifecycle model fits are descriptive; (8) concurrent publication, learned online scheduling, and post-training gains are explicitly out of scope (next system boundary); authentication/multi-tenancy/network transport and MCP as an experimental factor remain outside the evaluated stdio implementation.
facts.project_relevance: Directly on-topic for the agent-acceleration card's question of reducing repeated Read/Grep/Glob and of whether a code knowledge graph / repository index lowers end-to-end task cost: CodeNib is a concrete multi-view (lexical+dense+structural) repository-context serving system exposing search/navigation/context through MCP tools and LSP-shaped skills. The now-verified Q5 result (selected context policy uses 12.9-49.9% of paired grep/read tokens with localization preserved across five models) is the most project-actionable number: it quantifies the trajectory-token reduction a structured repository-context service delivers versus naive grep/read, directly addressing the card's 'reduce repeated Read/Grep' goal, with the explicit caveat that compaction is model-dependent (Haiku is worse than grep/read) and tokens are not cache-adjusted cost. The 8.67x/25.44x incremental graph/vector update speedups and the 4.72x static-vs-live navigation latency (on matching subset) give concrete lifecycle and per-operation cost numbers.

facts.title: A CXL Memory Rack for Multi-Turn LLM Serving
facts.event_hint: HyMCache: a CXL memory rack for multi-turn LLM serving built from cost-efficient CXL-hybrid memory (CXL-HM: small in-device DRAM + large SSD-backed capacity behind a CXL interface), using request-level prefix prefetching and opportunistic write buffering to stage latency-critical KV reads in device DRAM; evaluated on a real CXL-HM prototype under single-aggregator (Llama-3.1-8B, LMSYS, 512 conversations, concurrency 32, up to 10 turns) and PD-disaggregated serving.
facts.problem: Long-context, multi-turn, and agentic LLM workloads increasingly reuse previously processed context, so KV-cache reuse is essential to cut redundant computation. But this reuse shifts the bottleneck to the memory tier that stores and serves reusable KV states at cluster scale: GPU HBM and host DRAM are too costly to scale to TB-scale shared context capacity, motivating remote tiers built from lower-cost, higher-capacity media. Conventional CMM-H devices treat internal DRAM as a transparent LRU cache, which mis-handles multi-turn KV access: LRU-induced refills let one-shot-wonder blocks occupy space that should hold upcoming prefix blocks, and dirty evictions interleave backend writebacks with read traffic, degrading effective read bandwidth. GPU prefix caching and LMCache local-CPU caching also lose effective reuse once the accumulated prefix working set exceeds their cache capacity (around Turn 3 for GPU prefix caching, around Turn 4 for LMCache local CPU in the single-node LMSYS run), because evicting an early block truncates the contiguous reusable prefix chain.
facts.mechanism: HyMCache uses CXL-HM (small in-device DRAM + large SSD-backed capacity behind a CXL interface) as an explicitly managed staging space for KV objects rather than a transparent LRU cache. It exploits the read-dominant, predictable, append-only nature of multi-turn KV-cache access. Two design points: (1) KV-object prefetching — multi-turn prefix-cache lookup reveals the ordered list of KV objects an inference request will consume, and the serving runtime passes this object-level access order to CXL-HM via an explicit prefetch interface so upcoming KV objects are staged in device DRAM before foreground remote reads arrive; (2) latency-hiding staging window with opportunistic write buffering for newly generated KV. LLM workers access the remote KV tier as remote memory through RDMA (prototype path) or a CXL switch-based fabric; the remote tier is exposed as a unified memory address space backed by one or more CXL-HM devices. HyMCache uses an opportunistic remote-insertion policy: if the remote CXL-HM write buffer is full and cannot accept additional RDMA writes, it skips the insertion and retries in later turns rather than stalling the serving path, making it less sensitive to transfer-buffer pressure than distributed-DRAM Mooncake.

evidence.claim: Headline serving comparison with explicit DRAM budget (Section 1, PDF Page 2): with the SAME DRAM budget of 64 GB per worker (256 GB total), HyMCache improves serving performance over local LMCache by 3.0x in single-node serving and 1.45x in PD-disaggregated serving. Compared with 1 TB distributed-DRAM Mooncake, HyMCache trades a 30% performance gap for a 16x reduction in DRAM usage.
evidence.value: 3.0x vs LMCache (single-node); 1.45x vs LMCache (PD-disaggregated) at 64 GB/worker, 256 GB total; ~30% lower vs 1TB Mooncake at 16x less DRAM
evidence.baseline: local LMCache (64 GB/worker, 256 GB total same DRAM budget); 1 TB distributed-DRAM Mooncake
evidence.condition: real CXL-HM prototype, single-aggregator and PD-disaggregated serving
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 2 (Section 1 Introduction, paragraph following abstract)

evidence.claim: Single-node serving overall performance (Figure 11, Llama-3.1-8B, LMSYS, 512 multi-turn conversations, concurrency 32, up to 10 turns, decode max tokens=1 to isolate prefix reuse): GPU prefix caching loses effective reuse around Turn 3 and LMCache local-CPU caching around Turn 4 (once accumulated prefix working set exceeds cache capacity, LRU evicts an early block and truncates the contiguous reusable prefix chain). HyMCache preserves reusable prefix KV blocks in the CXL-HM tier and maintains a cache hit rate close to 90% across turns, avoiding the recomputation-driven latency growth that drives baselines back toward the recomputation curve.
evidence.value: HyMCache ~90% cache hit rate across turns; GPU prefix caching loses reuse ~Turn 3; LMCache local CPU ~Turn 4
evidence.baseline: Recomputation; GPU Prefix Caching (T1); LMCache (T1 + local DRAM)
evidence.condition: Llama-3.1-8B, LMSYS, 512 conversations, concurrency 32, up to 10 turns, decode max=1

evidence.claim: Transfer-buffer sensitivity vs distributed-DRAM Mooncake (Figure 10, Section 6.2 narrative): with the same 10 GB of additional host DRAM per node as a transfer buffer, Mooncake suffers severe transfer-buffer pressure — many remote KV insertions fail to complete in time, lowering effective KV reuse and breaking the contiguous prefix chain in later turns, so performance approaches the recomputation baseline even with a longer transfer timeout. HyMCache is less sensitive (its opportunistic remote-insertion policy skips and retries rather than stalling) and shows similar performance beyond a 10 GB transfer-buffer budget; Mooncake recovers only as the transfer-buffer budget increases.
evidence.value: Mooncake approaches recomputation at 10 GB transfer buffer; HyMCache insensitive beyond 10 GB
evidence.condition: varying per-node transfer-buffer host DRAM budget; same 10 GB/node starting point

evidence.claim: Prefetching microbenchmark (Figure 13a): on heavy random-read requests to the remote CXL-HM tier managed by HyMCache, enabling prefetching improves performance by 37% vs prefetch-off.
evidence.value: +37% with prefetching (microbenchmark random reads)
evidence.condition: heavy random-read microbenchmark against remote CXL-HM tier

evidence.claim: Workload motivation (Section 3): multi-turn KV-cache access is read-dominant, predictable, and append-only; conventional CMM-H LRU management mis-handles it — LRU refills leave one-shot-wonder blocks occupying space needed for upcoming prefix blocks, and dirty evictions interleave backend writebacks with reads, degrading effective read bandwidth. This motivates treating CXL-HM internal DRAM as an explicitly managed staging space rather than a transparent cache. KV-cache tiers framed via NVIDIA's G1-G4 hierarchy (G1 GPU HBM, G2 system DRAM via LMCache/Mooncake, G3 local SSD, G4 shared remote storage via NVMe-oF/RDMA/DPU).
evidence.value: multi-turn KV access read-dominant/predictable/append-only; LRU + dirty eviction degrade CMM-H read bandwidth; G1-G4 tier framing
evidence.condition: multi-turn LLM serving KV-cache access pattern analysis

facts.evaluation_context: Hardware: a real CXL-HM prototype (small in-device DRAM + large SSD-backed capacity behind a CXL interface); remote KV tier accessed as remote memory via RDMA (prototype example path) or CXL switch-based fabric; one or more CXL-HM devices forming a unified address space. DRAM budget for the LMCache comparison: 64 GB per worker, 256 GB total, held equal. Mooncake comparator: 1 TB distributed-DRAM, with a per-node transfer-buffer host-DRAM budget varied (10 GB starting point). Single-node serving workload: Llama-3.1-8B on LMSYS dataset, 512 multi-turn conversations, concurrency 32, up to 10 turns, decode max tokens=1 to isolate prefix reuse and prefill-side latency. Baselines: Recomputation, GPU Prefix Caching (T1), LMCache (T1 + local DRAM), Redis-only (T1 + Redis 64 GB), LMCache + Redis (T1 + local 64 GB + Redis 64 GB), and 1 TB distributed-DRAM Mooncake. Prefetch microbenchmark: heavy random reads against the remote CXL-HM tier. KV-cache tiering framed via NVIDIA G1-G4 hierarchy.
facts.limitations: The supplement confirms the DRAM budget (64 GB/worker, 256 GB total) behind the 3.0x/1.45x vs LMCache headline, the Mooncake config (1 TB distributed DRAM), and the single-node workload (Llama-3.1-8B, LMSYS, 512 conversations, concurrency 32, up to 10 turns, decode max=1). However, the absolute per-config throughput (tokens/s or req/s) and absolute P99 TTFT/P99 E2E latency values are still only available as Figure 11/12 axis ranges and curves, not as a per-turn numeric table, so the precise per-turn magnitudes behind the 3.0x/1.45x ratios are read off the figures. The single-node serving workload caps decode tokens at 1 to isolate prefix reuse, so the result does not directly represent decode-heavy or agentic multi-tool workloads. Prototype uses RDMA as the example access path; the CXL switch-fabric variant is described but its separate measurements are not in the visible evidence. Absolute CXL-HM device DRAM/SSD capacities, device count, and SSD media type (TLC/QLC) are not pinned in the visible evidence. Single-prototype scope; no multi-rack, concurrency-scaling beyond 32/64, or failure-mode evaluation is visible. The PD-disaggregated serving absolute numbers (vs only the LMCache baseline at the same DRAM budget) are less exposed than the single-node figures.
facts.project_relevance: Relevant to the cross-region / Agent-Cache card's question of how to store, move, and reuse KV-cache (and by extension reusable agent context) at cluster scale using lower-cost, higher-capacity media: HyMCache is a concrete CXL-HM rack that treats device DRAM as an explicitly managed staging space for predictable, append-only multi-turn KV access, using request-level prefix prefetching to hide SSD latency. The now-confirmed 16x-DRAM-reduction vs 1 TB Mooncake at a 30% performance cost (and 3.0x/1.45x over LMCache at equal 64 GB/worker DRAM budget) is a directly relevant cost/capacity tradeoff point for TB-scale shared context. The transfer-buffer sensitivity finding (distributed-DRAM Mooncake needs substantial extra local host DRAM as a transfer buffer, while HyMCache's opportunistic insertion is insensitive) is a concrete data-point on the consistency/buffering overhead the card asks about. The prefetching design (object-level access order revealed by prefix-cache lookup, passed to the device) is a concrete instance of the card's 'prefetch and placement to reduce latency' lever. Caveat: the result is single-turn-reuse KV (decode capped at 1) rather than WAN cross-region, so it speaks to shared-tier capacity more than to WAN RTT tradeoffs.

facts.title: AReaL-DTE: Sparse Policy-Weight Transfer for Online Agentic Reinforcement Learning
facts.event_hint: AReaL-DTE: a snapshot-free Delta Transfer Engine for online agentic RL that exploits inference-visible weight sparsity (<2% of BF16 elements change between consecutive policy versions) to make frequent policy-weight synchronization between training and rollout workers sparse across the full data path (construction, layout translation, transfer, application).
facts.problem: Online agentic RL with micro-services separates policy training from rollout generation, making frequent policy-weight synchronization a critical systems overhead. Shared storage connects these services across clusters, but vanilla dense synchronization incurs model-scale construction/transfer/application cost. Existing sparse/checkpoint-oriented approaches (e.g., PULSE) still retain a previous-model checkpoint and materialize complete intermediates to bridge heterogeneous training (Megatron-LM/FSDP) and inference (vLLM/SGLang) layouts (different parameter names, fusion/permutation rules, dtypes, TP/PP/DP/EP layouts). For a policy with N inference-visible elements, a dense refresh constructs, stages, transfers, and applies O(N) values even when the new policy differs at only a small fraction of positions.
facts.mechanism: AReaL-DTE is a snapshot-free Delta Transfer Engine that translates inference-visible weight sparsity into end-to-end efficiency. (1) On-demand reconstruction of overwritten weights by inverting AdamW updates (streaming AdamW inversion), avoiding a persistent historical snapshot. (2) Streams reconstructed and current parameters through converter-aligned BF16 change detection (after aligned conversion to the receiver's layout). (3) Remaps changed elements directly into receiver-local coordinates and delivers receiver-specific updates. Two transports: manifest-committed sparse transfer through shared storage (OSS) across clusters, and a deadlock-safe two-round protocol within a cluster followed by direct scatter-application to inference shards. Preserves layout translation while avoiding a complete-model representation for each refresh; relies on the surrounding control/storage layer for version ordering and consistency. Does not change the rollout schedule, RL algorithm, or consistency policy.

evidence.claim: Cross-cluster E2E synchronization latency (Table 2a, Qwen3-30B-A3B, derived as T_same,disk + T_upload,p50 + T_download,p50 over Alibaba OSS, Zstd-compressed, bandwidth 0.1/1/10 Gbps): AReaL-DTE 477.47/71.31/30.70 s on GSM8K vs ByteCheckpoint 8741.18/1080.12/314.05 s and PULSE 544.86/140.90/99.43 s. Speedups up to 19.9x over ByteCheckpoint and 3.2x over PULSE (the PULSE gap widens with bandwidth, reaching 3.2x at 10 Gbps).
evidence.value: Qwen3-30B-A3B GSM8K: 477.47/71.31/30.70 s (0.1/1/10 Gbps); up to 19.9x vs ByteCheckpoint, 3.2x vs PULSE
evidence.baseline: ByteCheckpoint (dense complete-state checkpoint); PULSE (sparse changed-values but retains previous checkpoint)
evidence.condition: Qwen3-30B-A3B, 16 H200 GPUs, storage-mediated cross-cluster, Alibaba OSS, Zstd, 0.1/1/10 Gbps

evidence.claim: Same-cluster E2E synchronization latency (Table 3, Qwen3-8B): AReaL-DTE synchronizes Qwen3-8B in 2.77-2.87 s, yielding speedups up to 7.6x over ByteCheckpoint-NCCL and 7.4x over PULSE-NCCL; benefit comes from constructing receiver-specific sparse updates and applying them directly to destination shards. (Abstract reports up to 7.6x and 7.4x within a cluster.)
evidence.value: Qwen3-8B same-cluster 2.77-2.87 s; up to 7.6x vs ByteCheckpoint-NCCL, 7.4x vs PULSE-NCCL
evidence.baseline: ByteCheckpoint-NCCL; PULSE-NCCL (direct NCCL and disk-mediated variants)
evidence.condition: Qwen3-8B, 8 H200 GPUs, same high-bandwidth cluster, AReaL-DTE direct sparse point-to-point path

evidence.claim: Transferred data volume: on Qwen3-30B-A3B AReaL-DTE produces Zstd-compressed sparse files of only 2.53-2.87 GB vs ~44.5 GB for ByteCheckpoint's compressed dense files (16.3x smaller on average), even though <2% of weights change, because every sparse entry stores both an int32 index and a BF16 value. On Qwen3-8B, AReaL-DTE reduces average Zstd-compressed artifact size by 19.7x relative to ByteCheckpoint.
evidence.value: Qwen3-30B-A3B sparse 2.53-2.87 GB vs dense ~44.5 GB (16.3x smaller); Qwen3-8B 19.7x smaller vs ByteCheckpoint; <2% weights change
evidence.condition: Zstd compression, <2% BF16 weight elements change between consecutive policy versions

evidence.claim: Peak memory (Table 2b, Qwen3-30B-A3B cross-cluster): AReaL-DTE GPU 71.52-71.96 GB / CPU 37.44-40.75 GB vs ByteCheckpoint GPU ~121 GB / CPU ~121-125 GB and PULSE GPU ~128-129 GB / CPU ~138-140 GB. AReaL-DTE reduces peak GPU memory by at least 40% and peak CPU memory by at least 66% relative to storage-mediated baselines (abstract reports ~41% GPU / >=87% CPU in same-cluster Qwen3-30B-A3B). Same-cluster Qwen3-8B peak CPU memory 3.45-3.48 GB vs 34.08-34.16 GB (ByteCheckpoint-NCCL) and 36.09-36.53 GB (PULSE-NCCL).
evidence.value: Qwen3-30B-A3B GPU ~71 GB vs ~121/~128 GB; CPU ~37-40 GB vs ~121-125/~138-140 GB; >=40% GPU, >=66% CPU reduction (cross-cluster); same-cluster Qwen3-8B CPU 3.45-3.48 GB
evidence.condition: Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-8B, H200 GPUs, peak memory during construction/staging/communication/application
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 11 (Table 2b); PDF Page 12 (Section 5.3, 5.4); PDF Page 13 (same-cluster Qwen3-8B CPU)

evidence.claim: Training-loop overhead (Figure 4, normalized as T_weight_sync / T_step_without_weight): at 10 Gbps AReaL-DTE overhead is 0.68-0.99x the policy-training time across the four workloads (Qwen3-30B-A3B 0.92-0.99x; Qwen3-8B 0.68-0.99x), whereas ByteCheckpoint and PULSE still incur 5.75-6.56x and 2.14-2.37x respectively. AReaL-DTE reduces weight synchronization from a dominant bottleneck to a cost comparable to or lower than the remaining training step.
evidence.value: at 10 Gbps AReaL-DTE 0.68-0.99x training time vs ByteCheckpoint 5.75-6.56x and PULSE 2.14-2.37x
evidence.condition: cross-cluster, 10 Gbps, normalized to training-step time excluding weight sync

facts.evaluation_context: Hardware: NVIDIA H200 GPUs; Qwen3-8B uses 8 GPUs, Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE) uses 16 GPUs. Models span dense (Qwen3-8B) and mixture-of-experts (Qwen3-30B-A3B) architectures. Workloads: four online RL datasets (GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH-500, LogiQA). Deployment: same-cluster (one high-bandwidth cluster, AReaL-DTE direct sparse point-to-point; baselines use direct NCCL and disk-mediated variants) and cross-cluster (training and rollout workers do not share an NCCL group; all methods use storage-mediated paths via Alibaba Cloud OSS with Zstd compression; effective inter-cluster bandwidths 0.1/1/10 Gbps). Cross-cluster latency is DERIVED as T_same,disk + T_upload,p50(B) + T_download,p50(B) (median storage-transfer times), not a direct end-to-end measurement. Baselines: ByteCheckpoint (dense complete-state checkpoint, parallelism-independent representation, load-time remapping) and PULSE (transfers changed BF16 values but retains previous checkpoint). Metrics: E2E synchronization latency (construction+communication+application for same-cluster; derived for cross-cluster) and peak GPU/CPU memory during construction/staging/communication/application.
facts.limitations: The cross-cluster E2E latency is a DERIVED metric (T_same,disk + median upload + median download over OSS), not a direct end-to-end measurement of a real cross-cluster run; p50 storage-transfer times hide tail behavior and OSS-specific dynamics. Only two baselines (ByteCheckpoint, PULSE) are compared; other relevant systems (TensorHub reference-oriented transfer, ROSE shard/sparsity-aware transfer, DORA multi-version, Laminar relay workers, Weave) are discussed as related work but not benchmarked. RL correctness/staleness impact is out of scope: AReaL-DTE optimizes the data-plane synchronization operation, not the rollout schedule, RL algorithm, or consistency policy, so any effect of sparse/asynchronous publication on training convergence is not measured here. Evaluation is limited to two Qwen3 models and four math/code/QA RL datasets; other model families and non-RL workloads are not covered. The <2% changed-weight fraction is workload-dependent and may not hold for other RL algorithms or training regimes. Absolute synchronization latency at 10 Gbps still equals 0.68-0.99x of the training step, so weight sync remains a non-trivial fraction of the loop even with AReaL-DTE.
facts.project_relevance: Relevant to the cross-region card's question of how compression, incremental/delta transfer, and placement reduce bandwidth and latency for moving large model/cache state across clusters: AReaL-DTE is a concrete snapshot-free delta-transfer engine that exploits <2% per-step weight sparsity to cut transferred volume 16.3x-19.7x (Zstd-compressed sparse vs dense) and cut cross-cluster sync latency up to 19.9x (vs ByteCheckpoint) / 3.2x (vs PULSE) at 10 Gbps, reducing weight-sync overhead to <=the training-step time. The on-demand AdamW-inversion reconstruction (avoiding a persistent historical snapshot) and receiver-local coordinate remapping are concrete instances of the card's 'incremental transfer + placement' levers for bridging heterogeneous layouts. Caveat for project use: the cross-cluster number is a derived metric over OSS, not a direct WAN measurement, and the workload is policy-weight sync for RL post-training rather than KV-cache or agent-cache transfer; nonetheless it is a directly relevant technique for making frequent cross-cluster state publication cheap.

facts.title: Scaling Agentic AI Factories Through Extreme Co-Design with NVIDIA BlueField
facts.event_hint: NVIDIA BlueField-4 / Vera BlueField-4 STX + DOCA platform positioning for agentic AI factory data-path offload (context-memory via DOCA Memos).
facts.problem: Agentic inference extends beyond model execution into a distributed workflow of tool calls, retrieval, KV-cache persistence, policy checks, storage and network transfers; infrastructure services running on host CPUs contend with agent execution inside the reasoning loop and can stall tool execution, retrieval and validation even when GPU compute is available, while GPU memory pressure forces KV-cache eviction, recompute or context-length limits that trade latency, throughput and cost.
facts.mechanism: BlueField-4 DPU (up to 800 Gb/s Ethernet/InfiniBand, 64-core Grace CPU, LPDDR5X, PCIe Gen6) and the Vera BlueField-4 STX Storage Processor (Vera CPU + ConnectX-9 + up to 1.6 Tb/s Spectrum-X) run networking, storage, security, telemetry and control-plane services in a dedicated in-silicon domain outside the host. DOCA exposes these as programmable services: DOCA HBN (server-side L3/BGP on BlueField), BlueField ASTRA (Spectrum-X zero-trust multi-tenant bare-metal control point with ConnectX-9), DOCA Memos (cross-node KV-cache management/sharing), and DOCA security services (zero-trust access, policy, runtime visibility, isolation). The STX storage processor runs KV I/O, KV-metadata tracking, queue management, cache recall/pre-staging and tenant policy close to the storage/network path instead of presenting flash as block storage, powering the NVIDIA CMX context-memory tier between GPU memory and shared storage.

evidence.claim: BlueField-4 integrates up to 800 Gb/s Ethernet or InfiniBand, a 64-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, high-bandwidth LPDDR5X memory, PCIe Gen6, inline acceleration and the DOCA software platform.
evidence.value: up to 800 Gb/s; 64-core Grace CPU; PCIe Gen6; LPDDR5X
evidence.condition: BlueField-4 DPU specifications, Vera Rubin platform
evidence.source_locator: Section: BlueField powers the operating system of the AI factory

evidence.claim: Compared with BlueField-3, BlueField-4 doubles networking bandwidth, delivers up to 6x more compute performance, 4x memory capacity and more than 3x memory bandwidth.
evidence.value: 2x networking bandwidth; up to 6x compute; 4x memory capacity; >3x memory bandwidth
evidence.condition: BlueField-4 vs BlueField-3 (architectural comparison, no workload defined)
evidence.source_locator: Section: BlueField powers the operating system of the AI factory

evidence.claim: The Vera BlueField-4 STX Storage Processor combines the NVIDIA Vera CPU, ConnectX-9 SuperNIC, up to 1.6 Tb/s Spectrum-X Ethernet, NVMe storage access, accelerated data movement, in-silicon security and DOCA programmability.
evidence.value: up to 1.6 Tb/s Spectrum-X; ConnectX-9; Vera CPU
evidence.condition: STX storage processor specifications
evidence.source_locator: Section: BlueField powers the operating system of the AI factory

evidence.claim: DOCA Memos manages and shares KV cache across compute and storage nodes so context can be reused across long-context and agentic inference; KV-cache reuse reduces repeated prefill, context recomputation, GPU idle time and unnecessary data movement.
evidence.value: KV-cache reuse across compute and CMX data nodes
evidence.baseline: recompute/eviction of KV cache on GPU memory pressure
evidence.condition: long-context and agentic workloads via DOCA Memos + NVIDIA CMX context-memory tier
evidence.source_locator: Section: System-level capabilities of BlueField; Section: AI-native storage and context memory

evidence.claim: BlueField-4 operates as the infrastructure processor in the GPU compute tray for frontend (north-south) networking, host CPU offload, secure data access, management, observability and isolation, with higher frontend bandwidth and lower host CPU contention claimed to support more predictable inference latency and higher tokens per second per user.
evidence.value: more predictable inference latency; higher tokens per second per user (directional, no magnitude)
evidence.condition: directional benefit stated without a quantified benchmark
evidence.source_locator: Section: GPU compute: Securing and accelerating Rubin GPUs

facts.evaluation_context: NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform co-design: Rubin GPUs, Vera CPUs, NVLink scale-up, ConnectX-9 + Spectrum-X scale-out, BlueField-4 DPU, Vera BlueField-4 STX storage processor, NVIDIA CMX context-memory tier, DOCA software. Target workload is agentic AI factories (multi-turn agents, long-context reasoning, RAG, multi-agent). The evidence is architectural/positioning prose; no benchmark table, hardware configuration, measured latency/throughput/CPU-utilization numbers, or baseline workload are disclosed in the visible Evidence Pack.
facts.limitations: This is a vendor technical blog, not a measurement paper. The Evidence Pack exposes only architectural claims and directional benefits (higher GPU utilization, more predictable latency, lower cost per token, more tokens per watt, 2x/6x/4x/3x vs BlueField-3) with no workload-defined benchmark, no measured CPU-offload percentage, no end-to-end latency or throughput figures, and no deployment scale. The 6x/4x/3x comparisons are silicon-spec ratios versus BlueField-3, not agentic-workload results. Quantitative validation of KV-cache-reuse gain (tokens per second, power efficiency) is asserted but not measured in the visible text.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to the DPU inline-offload topic: BlueField-4 + DOCA Memos is a concrete instance of moving KV-cache management, storage metadata, security, telemetry and control-plane services into the DPU/storage-processor in-path domain rather than the host CPU, which is the project's core question of which data-path operations can run inline on a DPU and whether single-point offload can form an end-to-end gain. The CMX + DOCA Memos path is the most project-relevant抓手 for cross-domain KV-cache/context-memory offload; the next verification step is finding any measured CPU-offload, latency or tokens-per-second/watt numbers for agentic workloads under this stack.

evidence_gaps.question: Are there measured quantitative results for agentic workloads (CPU-offload percentage, end-to-end latency, tokens per second, tokens per watt, KV-cache reuse hit rate) on the BlueField-4 + DOCA Memos stack?
What is the concrete deployment scale or configuration for the claimed BlueField-4 gains inside a Vera Rubin AI factory?
